methodology_notes.boundary_applied: Per Ecosystem methodology, code-level diagnostics/debuggability intrinsic to the language design were excluded (reserved for Language Quality); only debugger/profiler product maturity and IDE/editor tooling maturity were scored here.
methodology_notes.search_budget_used: 3 of 5 substantive searches; remaining budget calls returned no new content and were not used for evidence.
methodology_notes.sharding: This is a language-sharded Task Packet restricted to Swift only, per Assigned languages. Requirement value objects therefore carry only the Swift key; the runner is responsible for merging this shard with the other 9 language shards for these same two metric IDs before aggregation.

reasoning: LLDB is the default, deeply integrated debugger for Xcode and Swift, supporting breakpoints, stepping, variable/memory inspection, call-stack analysis, and arbitrary expression execution at a paused frame.

Swift's debugger REPL shares the language's full expression evaluator, so debugger expressions have access to the full range of Swift language features and consistent result formatting, giving unusually deep language-aware inspection compared to many other debuggers.

LLDB is cross-platform, known to work on macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, NetBSD and Windows across i386/x86-64/ARM, and is also the default debugger for Xcode 5+ and is reused by Android Studio, indicating broad ecosystem trust.

Outside Xcode, the official swiftlang/vscode-swift extension provides debugging via a dependency on the LLDB DAP extension, giving a first-party Debug Adapter Protocol path for VS Code users on any supported OS.

Xcode's Instruments provides mature, first-party profiling: Time Profiler pinpoints performance bottlenecks, and the Memory Graph Debugger visually presents objects and their relationships to help find retain cycles and leaks, alongside a View Debugger for 3D UI hierarchy inspection.

This profiling depth (Time Profiler, Memory Graph Debugger, View Debugger) is presented together with LLDB/breakpoints as Xcode's core debugging toolset, reflecting a cohesive, mature first-party stack; the main gap is that Instruments itself is Xcode/macOS-only, so non-Apple platforms lack an equivalently deep first-party profiler, which is reflected in the cross-platform-availability dimension.
metric.debugger_profiler_support.rubric: Frozen 0-100 rubric, four equally-weighted dimensions applied identically to all languages: (1) default debugger integration depth (breakpoints, expression evaluation, backtraces/REPL); (2) profiler tooling sophistication (CPU/time profiling, memory analysis, domain-specific instrumentation); (3) cross-platform/cross-editor availability of the debugger; (4) maturity/reliability track record. Each dimension scored 0-25 and summed.

reasoning: Xcode is Apple's first-party IDE bundling autocomplete, refactoring, live SwiftUI previews, an integrated debugger, and Instruments profiling in one product, and reviewers describe it as an all-in-one solution combining coding, previews, debugging, testing, the simulator, Instruments, and signing/distribution.
Xcode 16 added further coding-intelligence and debugging integration (e.g. Unified Backtrace View, Explicit Modules) as core pillars alongside Previews, the Simulator, and Debugging tools.

Official cross-editor support exists through SourceKit-LSP, which Apple/the Swift project ships and which powers the official swiftlang/vscode-swift VS Code extension (code completion, code actions, diagnostics) rather than relying only on an unofficial community package.

Cross-platform reach is real but has friction: prior to Swift 6.1 a manual `swift build` was required to populate the SourceKit-LSP index before language features worked, and users on Linux have reported completion/documentation not working in VS Code as of late 2025.

The main historical JetBrains alternative, AppCode, was sunsetted at the end of 2022 with only compatibility/security patches through 2023, leaving Xcode and the official VS Code extension as the practically maintained options rather than a broad multi-vendor IDE market.

User reviews of Xcode note real reliability friction: 'Code completion and SwiftUI previews can be hit-or-miss' and indexing can be slow and get stuck on large projects, alongside forum reports of code completion, Quick Help, and Refactor breaking after indexer failures.
metric.ide_editor_support_quality.rubric: Frozen 0-100 rubric, four equally-weighted dimensions applied identically to all languages: (1) first-party primary IDE completeness (autocomplete, refactoring, navigation, integrated build/run/debug/UI tooling); (2) multi-editor/cross-platform reach via LSP or equivalent; (3) breadth/currency of maintained alternative IDEs or editor plugins beyond the primary IDE; (4) reliability/maturity track record (issue reports, stability of indexing/completion). Each dimension scored 0-25 and summed.
